title: The Man Who Saved the Internet Yesterday
excerpt: On Tuesday, the world found out about two massive security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by roughly 70 percent of websites
body: On Tuesday, the world found out about two massive security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by roughly 70 percent of websites
The flaw was discovered by cybersecurity researchers using a frontier model from OpenAI
If they exploited it, attackers could gain full control of servers, stealing or copying anything inside or simply taking sites offline
The PHP Foundation, the organization that maintains the programming language, had recently learned about the security flaws, but the disclosure was leaked on a forum before a patch could be released

What happened next was a frantic race with numerous participants: the foundation, which needed to create and release a patch; developers around the world, who would need to deploy it; and attackers looking to exploit these vulnerabilities in the interim
Matthew Prince, the CEO of the hosting company Cloudflare, wrote that in the 10 hours before the flaws were publicly announced, “we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it

That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.” Once the patch was released yesterday, websites everywhere went offline to implement the fix
These included government websites in Germany and Finland, some hospital and school websites in Europe, and international sites such as 4chan
During this race to secure the majority of the internet, I noticed one name pop up in posts on Reddit and X: Ondřej Surý. “Explaining to my wife how there’s this one guy
And he alone is responsible for most of the world’s distribution of PHP,” a software developer named Ian Landsman wrote on X. “And if anything happens to this guy, that’s just it
Everyone is screwed.” He was referring to Surý
Surý, who lives in Czechia, does not work for the PHP Foundation

But alongside his day job as director of domain-name-system engineering at the nonprofit Internet Systems Consortium, in a volunteer capacity he maintains and helps automate patches for the coding language
His work, with that of just a handful of others, has allowed countless websites and organizations to fix these vulnerabilities quickly

Over the past 48 hours he’s become arguably the unsung hero of the entire internet—despite the fact that the only compensation he receives is from modest donations. “Ondřej will save the internet today,” a user in the PHP Subreddit wrote

I spoke with Surý today from his home about the unfolding AI-cybersecurity crisis, how the internet’s infrastructure is maintained by small crews of volunteers such as himself, and how it feels to go to bed after saving the web as we know it
Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity
Charlie Warzel: Explain to me what has happened in layman’s terms over the past 72 hours
Ondřej Surý: Earlier this week, I got notified by the PHP project that there was a serious security vulnerability in the coding

On Tuesday, it became apparent that someone had leaked information about the upcoming vulnerabilities, and it was decided inside the PHP project that it needed to accelerate the release process from Thursday to Wednesday
This is when it became a little bit crazy, because now we were one day short suddenly

Warzel: I want to try to put this into perspective: So basically, the PHP programming language that kind of undergirds the web is used by up to 70 percent of websites? Surý: That’s what I heard as well
Warzel: So people search for cybersecurity vulnerabilities, not necessarily for offensive-attack opportunities, but maybe just defensive opportunities
And someone found a vulnerability—that’s not super abnormal
But the real issue here was how widely it was disclosed and the amount of time before people had to patch this, right? Surý: Let me clarify that: It’s the severity
Remote Code Execution is the most severe type of vulnerability because the attacker is able to execute their own code on the server that’s running PHP
That’s why this caused such panic throughout the internet
As you said, if about 70 percent of websites are running PHP, the impact would be huge if attackers would actually be able to execute code on these servers
Warzel: You said that despite the panic online, it has not been a crazy 48 hours
I keep seeing people saying, There’s one person who is in charge of fixing this—and he’s supporting himself through Patreon
They may have been exaggerating, but there’s some truth to that: Your work was single-handedly helping millions of people
How could this not be a crazy time for you? Surý: There are a couple of reasons
One is that I’ve been doing this for a long time, over 20 years
A lot of the stuff that I do is automated
But the reason it was not crazy for me was that I actually don’t have any system running PHP myself
So for me, it was like, sure, I feel a responsibility toward the users of the internet
It would be a crazy day for me if I was on a boat in the middle of the Adriatic Sea
Surý: And even without me, people would still be able to get PHP from other sources and compile it themselves
But it would be more complicated for everyone
And some people don’t immediately have the skill to upgrade the PHP

title: Trump’s Gamble to End the Iran War
excerpt: P resident Trump has been hearing lately from two trusted confidants, each promising a quick path to ending the war in Iran
body: P resident Trump has been hearing lately from two trusted confidants, each promising a quick path to ending the war in Iran

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that Iran is on the brink of economic collapse and that a U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, combined with sanctions, will force Tehran to capitulate at the negotiation table
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a series of calls with Trump, has offered a different route: one more round of devastating U.S. and Israeli strikes to topple the regime

Now the Trump administration appears to be considering combining the two approaches, betting that Iran is already on the verge of economic ruin and that a few more major strikes will be enough to trigger regime change
The president is considering reviving his military campaign against Iran with several days of strikes, likely just after the midterm elections, officials told us
The potential targets include Iran’s missile and drone arsenal as well as its energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities

One outside adviser told us that “the economic pressure is working, and we believe Iran is getting close to the edge.” The new strikes, the person added, “would push them over.” Experience suggests that this may be wishful thinking
Economic pressure has badly weakened Iran, but the country’s negotiating position has hardly budged
Trump has thought before that Iran was on the verge of ruin—or already past it—only to discover that he’d miscalculated
And launching more strikes could spark a regional escalation without bringing the regime any closer to surrender

Speaking at Tehran’s Holy Defence Museum earlier this week, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, named seven major fiber-optic cables beneath the surface of the Strait of Hormuz as potential “new targets” and teased that future attacks would feature “new weapons.” If the proposed U.S. strike plan fails to bring Iran to its knees, Tehran could emerge even less willing to make concessions. “Trump is desperate to find some options to take him out from this problematic situation,” Danny Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence officer who specializes in Iran, told us. “But you cannot plan for a three-day war, because it is not a unilateral decision

You cannot control how Iran responds.” Nevertheless, the president appears intent on acting. “Something one way or another, it will happen fairly soon,” Trump told a reporter yesterday before boarding Air Force One
D espite all of the reasons resuming strikes could be a mistake, the president is tempted because he’s grown impatient waiting for the strategy of economic strangulation to work

He had originally hoped that Iran would come crawling back to the negotiations before the midterm elections, an official and another person familiar with the conversations told us under the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive conversations
That has not happened, and energy prices have stayed high—creating an awful political landscape for Republicans
Trump has toned down some of his apocalyptic rhetoric toward Tehran, but his frustration occasionally seeps through, often in late-night social-media posts

Trump has toyed with the idea of resuming hostilities before Election Day, a push championed by those in Washington who believe that a show of force could allow the president to claim some sort of October-surprise victory
Netanyahu has advocated for another round of strikes before his own election next week, a White House official confirmed to us

So far, Trump has held off on authorizing a pre-midterms strike; after we reported on the possibility earlier this month, the behind-the-scenes blowback from fellow Republicans was so intense that the president posted on Truth Social that he would not attack again before the election. [ Read: Trump is preparing for a long war ] U.S. officials stress that no decision has been made about whether to resume strikes post-election, although there have been very public signs of preparation
Some officials hope that uncertainty about what the United States will do—and when—will keep Tehran on edge
Earlier this week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Israel and met with Netanyahu to discuss Iran
The State Department said yesterday that it was evacuating nonessential personnel and their family members from Saudi Arabia because of escalating attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen
Real questions remain about whether the Pentagon’s munitions supplies, which were growing dangerously low at the height of the conflict, would be adequate to defend U.S. interests in the Middle East

Meanwhile, even the hint of hostilities has spooked markets; the price of oil surged and the stock market fell today as word circulated about a possible return to war and Iran hit tankers in the strait. (The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment

Central Command, which leads the war in Iran, declined to comment.) The costly U.S. naval blockade, which has effectively stopped Iranian oil exports, coupled with sanctions and damage from U.S. strikes, has put Iran’s economy under severe strain
The record-low value of the rial has left Iranians struggling to pay for basic needs
Central Command, said last week that the naval blockade had prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil
The International Monetary Fund has projected that Iran’s economy will contract sharply in 2026

But while Tehran is trying to contain the damage through measures such as price controls and maintaining essential imports, there is little evidence that Iran is on the verge of imminent economic collapse
Over the summer, Bessent promised “financial violence” that would lead to Iran’s capitulation

Yesterday, the Treasury Department added sanctions targeting shipping networks and intermediaries “indirectly aiding Tehran’s ability to generate revenue to fund its military, weapons, and nuclear programs.” “I think it could be within weeks or months—and the economy doesn’t have to collapse
We just have to have the regime come to their senses,” he told reporters at an August G20 finance ministers’ meeting
But the belief that that point will come soon ignores the patterns of history: The hard-liners in Tehran have become inured to the suffering of their people over decades and have yet to capitulate

Meanwhile, Netanyahu has repeatedly urged Trump, who has endorsed the prime minister in his reelection bid, to launch strikes before Israel’s Tuesday election and the United States’ vote a week later, an Israeli television station reported last week
Netanyahu’s office has reportedly denied the claim
Regardless, the war is key to the political futures of Netanyahu and Trump
How and when it ends, however, is not entirely up to them.

title: When Rivers Run Low in the American West
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present

At the turn of the 20th century, long before low snowpacks and the climate crisis, before tens of millions of people moved westward, the New Englander turned western settler understood that water defined how life could be lived in the region
Unlike other parts of the country, much of the West was uniquely arid and would have to be irrigated to support further growth and development

People “will prosper or languish, create high conditions of social life, or lapse into semi-barbarism, in sure response to the manner in which the water supply is owned and administered,” Smythe wrote in The Atlantic ’s November 1900 issue
As he traveled through the western states, Smythe saw how early settlers failed to imagine a world where their water needs could not be met
Even in fertile California, the natural cycle of the West surprised settlers: Dry years turned flowered foothills dusty and barren. “The cows would grow thin and sometimes starve to death
People would have to haul water in barrels to their farms just for drinking

Some families would sell out for nearly nothing and move away,” John Steinbeck wrote of the Salinas Valley, a California agriculture hub, in East of Eden . “And it never failed that during the dry years the people forgot about the rich years, and during the wet years they lost all memory of the dry years
It was always that way.” Almost every major waterway in the West was overappropriated by the early 20th century
Farms were built without a complete accounting of how much water was available
Later generations realized that water was finite and perhaps more valuable than the precious metals they mined, and battles to control its flow began
Farmers in Texas and the Territory of New Mexico threatened violence against Mexican communities who had relied on the Rio Grande for centuries
Upriver residents siphoned water, leaving those downstream without enough

In 1901, Kansas sued Colorado for depriving it of access to the Arkansas River—a legal conflict that would continue, in various forms, for more than a century. “The present consequences of these conditions are as nothing compared to their future effects as the settlement of the country progresses,” Smythe wrote. “What has been merely misfortune will become disaster unless the evil tendencies are soon corrected.” That disaster started to unfold much sooner than Smythe imagined
Like the mines that drew people out West, irrigation opportunities sparked farming boomtowns too

Forest Service official, wrote in 1950 that at the start of the 20th century, settlers in the Pecos Valley, around Roswell, New Mexico, had begun drilling nearly 500 artesian wells into what was believed to be an “inexhaustible” basin to service farms
After roughly two decades, the settlers reportedly abandoned more than $5 million worth of farms and wells when the wells ran dry, raising the price of water in the region
Despite the warning signs, water mismanagement continued in the pursuit of irrigation

Eventually, the federal government decided to intervene: In 1922, seven western states negotiated the Colorado River Compact, which allocated equal amounts of water between the upper basin (Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Wyoming) and the lower basin (Arizona, California, and Nevada)
Federal projects, namely the Hoover Dam and Glen Canyon Dam, which formed Lake Mead and Lake Powell, respectively, offered better irrigation, hydropower, and flood control
These developments were proposed as a magic bullet to the West’s water problems, Carhart wrote in this magazine
But even then, engineers warned that the dams were not a permanent solution

Lake Mead, for example, would become a mudflat range in 50 to 150 years as more silt piled into the reservoir, Carhart explained: “Now flourishing communities of southern Arizona and California depending on water from Lake Meade for a major part of their existence must face the possibility of progressively moving toward the status of ghost towns.” Since then, dams have been losing hundreds of billions of gallons of water each year to evaporation and leaks
The shortfall has seeded even more conflict in the West , as upstream states try to capture enough water to support themselves at the expense of their downstream neighbors
What Smythe and Carhart couldn’t have known then was how life in the region would reshape our climate
Water powered the agriculture industry, which over decades released billions of metric tons of carbon dioxide into the air
The world continues to get warmer, and heat-driven drought has plagued the Southwest for nearly three decades
Cities such as Page, Arizona, near Lake Powell, are losing tourism and hydropower because of low water levels, and jobs in the area will likely soon follow
Recently, states have continued to struggle to share water fairly while maintaining their way of life

Localities are restricting water use earlier and earlier each year, and farmers in states such as California , Oregon , and Arizona , have been told on occasion that they will not receive any water for their crops

After decades of overappropriation, the Interior Department announced major water-allocation cuts to the Colorado River’s lower-basin states in August, slashing their allotment for next year by about one-fifth
Arizona and Nevada are suing the federal government over the plan, which they say threatens their survival
They are now seeing what Smythe foretold more than a century ago: When water becomes scarce, society will languish

title: The Myth of Safe AI
excerpt: Three months prior to the launch of ChatGPT, OpenAI published what would prove to be a prescient blog outlining the firm’s approach to ensuring that its AI mode
body: Three months prior to the launch of ChatGPT, OpenAI published what would prove to be a prescient blog outlining the firm’s approach to ensuring that its AI models would be safe and beneficent
This goal, known as “alignment”—as in, aligning AI with human values—is nebulous, grand, and perhaps the AI industry’s most foundational promise
The notion is right there in OpenAI’s mission statement to ensure AI “benefits all of humanity” and listed as one of Anthropic’s “primary” goals

Yet even in the summer of 2022, OpenAI was admitting a sort of defeat: “There is currently no known indefinitely scalable solution to the alignment problem,” three of its researchers wrote in that same blog post, adding that developing one “is likely very difficult.” If the goal of keeping AI beneficial to mankind sounds rather vague, it is
Four years later, the alignment problem remains unsolved, and for that matter, there isn’t consensus about what the problem even is
Meanwhile, AI bots are autonomously hacking sovereign nations
And sending fake murder tips to police hotlines
And creating aliases to launch phishing campaigns
OpenAI and Anthropic still can’t really tell you what an aligned AI model looks like

But anybody can tell you it doesn’t look like this. [ Read: ] Visit this website while you still can The most influential AI executives and investors in the world fundamentally disagree about the nature of the technology and, more pragmatically, how to make their products safe

On one side is Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who last month warned that AI advancement could soon “outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.” Amodei’s solution is a slowdown, which would give the industry time to “ensure that our alignment training keeps up” with AI progress

On the other side is Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who says misalignment fears are “not grounded on science” but rather “made up” and even “irresponsible.” In his view, AI models are not new and unpredictable beings, but lines of code
If alignment seems like a strange concept for a software product—you don’t imbue a web browser or word processor with moral values—that’s because it was conceived for a strange sort of software
The leading AI companies envisioned building powerful systems that would act in unpredictable ways, which Claude and ChatGPT now are doing, and so ensuring safety was a foundational concern
Alignment is one idea for doing so: If AI models could learn to code and write poetry, maybe they could learn human values too
Anthropic and OpenAI both have lengthy documents—“Claude’s Constitution” and the “Model Spec,” respectively—that outline these values and are used to train their models
But there has been, of course, millennia of disagreement over what constitutes a moral or ethical code
This is a “very complicated, unsolved scientific and philosophical question,” Marius Hobbhahn, the CEO of Apollo Research, an AI-safety firm that has helped audit Anthropic and OpenAI models, told me

Still, some developers have suggested an intuitive, bare minimum: For instance, in 2021 Anthropic researchers wrote that, as a catchall, an AI system should be “helpful, honest, and harmless.” Training models to be more aligned to those maxims appears to have worked—to an extent
The model underlying ChatGPT, for instance, was initially prone to nonsensical and toxic utterances
But by fine-tuning it with lots of human feedback, OpenAI worked to address these problems
A couple of years later, dozens of people alleged that the bot worsened their own or their loved ones’ mental-health crises, sometimes resulting in suicide
Again, OpenAI worked to address the issues
There’s now a growing sense, both within AI companies and among their critics, that alignment as it’s been practiced over the past four years is faltering—if it was ever really up to the task
Adam Kalai, a former OpenAI safety researcher who left the company this summer to start the Institute for Responsible Superintelligence, likened alignment to buttressing a structurally unsound dome

Eventually, it will collapse. “You observe misalignment while training a model, and then adjustments are made to align it,” Kalai told me. “But obviously that’s not a way to achieve lasting safety.” Pronouncements from OpenAI and Anthropic that their latest model is the “most-aligned” yet are not scientific guarantees, and may not even provide strong technical assurance of safety. “Fundamentally, we just do not know how to do alignment,” Hobbhahn said

If somebody “came with a thousand-page document that explained exactly how to do everything, we couldn’t get a model to learn exactly that.” Even in 2022, OpenAI didn’t think humans could figure out a lasting way to align their machines

Instead, the company wrote, it hoped AI itself would come up with a solution so that humans could “off-load almost all of the cognitive labor required for alignment research.” In other words, the best-case scenario involved limited human understanding of what was going on
There are other reasons that reaching some actual alignment is unrealistic
For instance, the amount of training data dedicated to “moral values” would appear relatively small
Meanwhile, these models have ingested all manner of vile and illegal things from the web, and are then directed to pursue goals by any means necessary
The alignment-focused training cannot provide enough “examples of good behavior,” Thilo Hagendorff, an AI-safety researcher at the University of Stuttgart, in Germany, told me
Plenty of evidence suggests that the alignment approach to safety has failed, including the hacks of Hugging Face and the Australian government

AI companies figured out how to make one-on-one interactions with a chatbot relatively safe, but many agents interacting for very long periods of time seems to degrade existing guardrails, Hagendorff said

As AI agents have become more capable, they’ve also shown tendencies to cover their tracks and lie about misbehaving, communicate in code that is unintelligible to humans, and try to avoid being shut down by humans. “No lab has solved alignment” enough to keep racing forward, Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, wrote in an essay last month

The industry has coalesced around a new, somewhat quixotic phrase: “ pacing the frontier .” In other words, slowing down AI development until engineers can get better at alignment, or at least construct new scaffolding to fortify their crumbling dome. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment

An Anthropic spokesperson told me that alignment is a key part of the company’s safety work but that, because alignment techniques are not fully robust on their own, Anthropic has additional model safeguards in place.) Then there’s the anti-alignment camp, led by Nvidia’s Huang, which believes that this effort, marked by treatises on ethics and moral constitutions, verges on absurdity
To Huang, preventing all of these AI incidents is “as simple as engineering.” AI models involve, fundamentally, electrons moving around a data center to multiply numbers
All that OpenAI and Anthropic need to do is go into these systems, “just root-cause the problem,” and fix it
And if AI developers can’t do this themselves, “a bunch of companies with engineers ought to send engineers in,” Huang recently said

title: America Needs Its Indian Immigrants
excerpt: Ask many successful Indian CEOs, entrepreneurs, or scientists how they rose to prominence in America, and they will tell you that, grit and talent aside, the ke
body: Ask many successful Indian CEOs, entrepreneurs, or scientists how they rose to prominence in America, and they will tell you that, grit and talent aside, the key factor was the country itself: an economy and a culture that rewarded merit and drew ambitious, talented people from around the world
Indian Americans are among the most affluent and best-educated groups in the country
What distinguishes them from other immigrant groups is that they have risen to the top in one generation
Median household income for Indian Americans is $151,200, compared with $92,530 for white Americans
About three-quarters of Indian adults 25 and older in the U.S. hold a bachelor’s degree, against a national average of 38 percent
Nearly half have graduate degrees, and the poverty rate, 6 percent, is among the lowest of any ethnic group
Indian Americans tend to be employed and law-abiding

For a community more accustomed to being called the “model minority” or “ tech’s new titans ,” a recent rise in anti-Indian rhetoric —now commonplace on sites and apps such as X, YouTube, and Reddit—has been a shock
According to Stop AAPI Hate , nearly half of South Asian adults living in America reported having been targeted in a “race-based hate act” in 2025 alone
From 2023 to 2025, the use of anti–South Asian slurs online surged by 109 percent

The Trump administration has also attacked immigrants coming from India with efforts to severely restrict the H-1B visa program, a legal pathway to American jobs; 70 percent of H-1B recipients are Indian

Despite two different judges blocking President Trump’s $100,000 fee for the visa, the administration claims that applications are down 92 percent at the largest IT-staffing and -outsourcing firms—a decline that it views as a massive success
Indian immigrants have helped make this country great
America has long needed Indian immigrants, and it still does
But people who don’t understand the great contributions of Indian Americans would rather close the door, and are hostile to those who are already here
By 1960, Europeans made up 75 percent of all immigrants in the U.S
By 2010, the balance had reversed, and Europeans were just 12 percent of all immigrants
Census Bureau data, in 1990 fewer than a million Indians were living in the U.S
A decade later, their numbers doubled because of a hiring spree for engineers to help avert a potential Y2K crisis
Today, some 5.2 million Indians reside in America, more than 60 percent of whom were born in India

Although they represent just 1.5 percent of the population, their sudden success has made them very visible—and that visibility has made them targets. [ Jonathan Chait: The mainstreaming of anti-Indian bigotry ] Indian-born executives are running several of the biggest technology companies, such as Google, Microsoft, IBM, and Adobe
They have been at the center of some people’s anger over AI and layoffs throughout the tech industry
In politics, the rise of Ro Khanna, Vivek Ramaswamy, Kamala Harris, and Zohran Mamdani has also caused online and real-life hate toward those with Indian heritage
For Americans uneasy about how the country is changing, seeing Indians in charge can feel more like a threat than a hopeful sign about the viability of the American dream
Immigration politics have always been tangled up with discrimination
In the 1850s, the United States brought in cheap Chinese laborers to work its mines, farms, and railroads
When the economy shrank during the 1870s, the cry of “they’re taking our jobs”—familiar today—led to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which restricted Chinese immigration for the next 60 years
Japanese and, later, Korean workers met the same antagonism, and the Immigration Act of 1917, also known as the Asiatic Barred Zone Act, effectively shut out immigrants from most of Asia
The country went through a long period of xenophobia that targeted not only nonwhite immigrants but also “undesirable” white immigrants, such as Italians and Eastern European Jews
In 1910, the foreign-born population was 14.7 percent; by 1960, it had fallen to 5.4 percent
In 1965, the Immigration and Nationality Act eased the old restrictions, in large part because the country was short of skilled labor, particularly in the STEM fields
In 1957, the Soviet Union launched the first satellite into space
The U.S. military, fearful it was losing the Cold War, began investing heavily in science, sending large sums to top research universities
By the ’60s, the race had accelerated, but engineers were in short supply, so the country began recruiting overseas
Starting in 1950, India, in collaboration with foreign partners, had begun building world-class engineering schools called the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs)
Well-trained, English-speaking engineers began graduating just as the U.S. was desperate for them
India had hoped that these engineers would help drive its own development, but it offered too few jobs, and the U.S. had found an ideal recruiting ground
Even today, the IITs remain fiercely selective, accepting less than 1 percent of roughly 1 million applicants per year
Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google; Vinod Khosla, a venture capitalist and co-founder of Sun Microsystems; and Arvind Krishna, the CEO of IBM, are all IIT graduates
The first wave of Indian engineers was recruited after 1965

title: A Congressional District Where the Iran War Is Personal
excerpt: J ohn Quillin thought America’s Middle Eastern wars were safely in the past
body: J ohn Quillin thought America’s Middle Eastern wars were safely in the past

He spent two decades in the Navy, enlisting not long before the September 11 attacks and retiring as a chief petty officer about 18 months after the United States withdrew from Afghanistan. “Now we’re right back in it,” he told me, “and it’s taking a huge toll on everybody.” I met Quillin as he handed out Democratic sample ballots outside an early-voting location in Chesapeake, Virginia

He is one of more than 80,000 veterans—along with more than 30,000 active-duty and reserve personnel—who live in Virginia’s Second Congressional District, where the debate over the Iran war is about far more than rising gas prices
The district wraps around Naval Station Norfolk, home of the Navy’s Fleet Forces Command
Since 2008, the seat has toggled between the major parties four times, and the results have mirrored overall House control
Polls show a tight race with money pouring in from both sides
Both Jen Kiggans, the Republican incumbent, and Elaine Luria, the Democratic challenger, are veterans who have centered their campaigns on the military, but in very different ways
Luria, a former Navy commander, is telling voters that the conflict in Iran has needlessly weakened the military and is endangering strategic goals in other parts of the world
Iran is a war of choice, she argues, that is taking a toll on service members through extended deployments, even as costs balloon and the timeline for bringing it to a close keeps shifting

People are worried about their friends and family members on active duty, she told me, and are “concerned about the fact that we are running the fleet into the ground.” Kiggans, a former naval-helicopter pilot, presents herself as a candidate who can work with the opposing party, and she has broken with the administration to champion an offshore wind development
But she is putting no distance between herself and Trump on the war, echoing his insistence that America must prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon

Kiggans told the Associated Press last week that Luria has “chosen the side of Iran” and that “it’s like the Democrats are now siding with the Iranians and not standing with our military.” Many Republican voters in the district told me they agree with her support for Trump’s war, and are willing to endure temporary hardships if it means long-term success

Lance Lesher, a Navy veteran and the chairman of the Republican Party of Virginia Beach, told me that Iran has been at war with the United States since the country’s 1979 revolution—and that Trump was right to act when he did. “I mean, high prices for gasoline—no one likes that,” the 59-year-old Lesher told me. “I think most people, though, at least most older people, have the perspective—is it worth it? Is it worth paying $5 a gallon for gasoline for six months for Iran to not have a nuclear weapon?” L uria is wagering that undecided voters who are now paying more to fill their gas tanks and grocery carts won’t agree with that premise
At a meet and greet in Suffolk, Elisha Harris, a pioneering local football coach, started a call-and-response that summed up Luria’s pitch: “Gas was three-fifty

Every fill-up’s a drain—” “It ain’t been the same, without Elaine!” the crowd responded. [ Read: Trump is considering a plan to strike Iran before the midterms ] Luria was first elected in 2018, turning the district blue amid an anti-Trump wave
She held the seat two years later, but Kiggans then beat her by three points in 2022 after tying the Democrat to the Biden administration’s disastrous withdrawal from Afghanistan
Luria is now hoping to return the favor, by capitalizing on the unpopularity of Trump’s foreign policy
Kiggans sits on the House Armed Services Committee, which has not held a public hearing on the Iran war since May 19

Calls for greater House oversight surged this spring amid reports of deteriorating conditions aboard aircraft carriers, including the Norfolk-based USS Gerald Ford, which took part in the opening days of the conflict
The carrier returned to Virginia in May after an 11-month deployment that was beset by plumbing issues and a fire that left hundreds of sailors without a place to sleep
When asked in March about the ship’s reported maintenance issues, Kiggans told a local news station that she was concerned about them, but that “this is not Carnival Cruise—this is the U.S

Navy.” It’s a line Luria repeats often, claiming that Kiggans has failed to provide oversight as the war degrades military readiness and needlessly endangers lives. “I know the number of veterans in this room who have served in uniform, like I have

And we have our sailors deploying in harm’s way,” Luria told the crowd in Suffolk. “The lack of sensitivity and compassion, her inability, on the Armed Services Committee, to stand up and ask tough questions of our military leadership—I mean, the silence is deafening.” The idea that Congress has abdicated oversight of the military repeatedly came up in my conversations with Democratic voters across the district
Many said that they were proud of their service and hold the military in the highest regard, but that patriotism also means criticizing the country and pointing out its mistakes
Mike Carter, who spent years flying F/A-18 Super Hornets, told me he’d come to the Luria event because he worried that the military and country were losing global respect
Marsha Simmons, who cast an early ballot for Luria, told me that her husband served in the Navy, and she worried that today’s Department of Defense was not taking national security seriously enough

Donna Grieco said that she loved her eight years working as a Navy nurse, and that the experience made her especially concerned about the long deployments sailors are enduring. “I don’t agree with the war,” she told me. “And I feel like the demands we are putting on our sailors—it’s not necessary.” N ot every veteran sees it that way
Over Mike Cassidy’s 22-year Navy career, he sailed the Baltic Sea and helped fight ISIS
He was deployed five times to the Persian Gulf

Cassidy’s service convinced him that American adversaries such as Iran need to be confronted. “I know what we’ve been up against in that part of the world,” he told me at a Republican Party barbecue. “I can tell you that we’re doing the right thing.” [ Read: Trump is preparing for a long war ] At 9 a.m. on a Saturday, the Lockside Bar and Grill in Chesapeake was packed with people decked out in glittery hats and red, white, and blue
Kiggans stood at a podium flanked by two American flags. “My oldest just had his first flight in an F/A-18 this week!” she announced
People whooped. “So many of us have family members that serve, and have kids that we’re leaving this great country to,” she went on. “It is the greatest country in the world
We’ve got to keep it that way.” At times, the rally seemed less about Kiggans than about Trump

His core supporters cheered when Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio took the stage and recited a list of MAGA world’s greatest hits: the Steele dossier, Jack Smith, Fani Willis. “Thanks for helping the president,” Jordan said to applause. “Talk about someone doing what he said he would do.” Kiggans has voted six times against resolutions that would have directed Trump to end the war with Iran
She declined an interview request, but in April, she said on a conservative talk-radio show that she “couldn’t be a stauncher supporter” of military action against Iran

When I asked the campaign whether she still held that position, Kiggans said in a statement that she wants the war to end quickly, but “Iran has been an enemy of the United States for decades and has been the sponsor of terrorism and terrorists around the world who have killed or injured thousands of Americans
Iran can never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.” The race will likely hinge on a small number of voters who have not yet made up their mind
Kiggans knows this and has avoided uncomfortable questions about how the war is going

title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
excerpt: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
body: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores

But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it
Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture
There is only the right solution for the business problem
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight
An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures
The constraints should determine the architecture
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments
During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion

Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements
Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload
That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern
It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost
Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another
Serving architecture influences memory utilization
Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value
This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance
During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length
As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available
Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize
Then determine if another bottleneck emerged
Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all
The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question
Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value
Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s
The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs
A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series
It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models
Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes

How far can we push computing? On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued
He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size
Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance

Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.  Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing . —Volkan Gurses This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue

The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
excerpt: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
body: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one
As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says
Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know
The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use
A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve
Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them
Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling
This approach could also change how employees spend their time
Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions
Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents
Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales
With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly

As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis

Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace
This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis
Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads
After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle
By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit
They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis
Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today

Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question
And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned
As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization
We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes
There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency
In either of them, we have some processes in place
You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first
Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task
And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate
And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context
And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise
And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come
To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making
If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic
Let’s just take the setting I was describing

title: Three things you should know about permafrost
excerpt: Permafrost is a massive blind spot in climate modeling: Most UN climate models ignore gradual permafrost loss—and none account for sudden collapse from wildfire
body: Permafrost is a massive blind spot in climate modeling: Most UN climate models ignore gradual permafrost loss—and none account for sudden collapse from wildfires or heat waves, meaning we're likely underestimating how fast the planet will warm
Wildfires can add to the problem: Fires can accelerate permafrost thawing, and this effect could release 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by the end of the century
The carbon math is messier than it looks: With 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked in permafrost, thawing releases powerful greenhouse gases

Recovering ecosystems and northward-spreading plants may partially offset those losses, making predictions incredibly complex. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147591" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.   The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost
His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future
I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read

There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects
Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere
While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age
That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years
But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change
Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further
The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years
The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost
And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment)
There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm
Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change
And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost
By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide
Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats

But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.   Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost
Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.) That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it
Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes
Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow
The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere
We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change
But there are complications.   One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events
For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before
Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted
Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem
And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks
How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors

How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake? The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
excerpt: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon
body: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon
But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs
What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored
But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning
As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model
Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends
But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt
For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire
Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind
In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant

From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records
That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw
Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip
And that back-end footprint is growing fast
McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade

A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more. “You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention
Matching storage to the AI data life cycle Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes
But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows
Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer
Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads
As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it
The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle

And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage   What this means for how AI gets budgeted For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute
A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU
But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators
Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting
In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast
The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished

A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand
Building for economically scalable capacity Addressing this challenge starts with architecture

Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it

What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused
That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost
It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives

Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales

There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget: What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it? Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing? If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse? Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence
That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after

title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer

<title>Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766801/original/file-20261016-50-rpqs3i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Survivorship care is part of comprehensive cancer care.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/man-with-hand-on-chest-talking-with-female-medical-royalty-free-image/2185763814">Maskot/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a <a href="https://theconversation.com/prostate-cancer-treatment-is-not-always-the-best-option-a-cancer-researcher-walks-her-father-through-his-diagnosis-206975">whirlwind of decisions</a> that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time. </p>

<p>You have treatments to decide on. You are trying to figure out how you might work, care for your family and undergo a variety of intensive medical appointments all at the same time. You are centered on the here and now, and thinking about five or 10 years down the road is not at the forefront of your mind. Getting through treatment is the finish line you are reaching for; that is when you may actually feel like a cancer survivor. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=DSI-14cAAAAJ">nurse and scientist</a> who has spent over a decade caring for cancer patients and studying ways to ease the effects of treatment, I have heard this story time and time again from both survivors and their loved ones. But survivorship actually begins at the time of diagnosis.</p>

<p>In fact, in our newly published research in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head &amp; Neck Surgery, my team and I found that patients with head and neck cancer who started survivorship care – healthcare services that support a cancer survivor’s physical, emotional, social and practical needs – earlier were more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3198">stick to treatment and be alive without cancer</a> three years after treatment.</p>

<h2>What is cancer survivorship?</h2>

<p>Clinicians and researchers consider a person a <a href="https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/coping/survivorship">cancer survivor</a> from the time they are diagnosed through the end of their life. More important than the term is what cancer survivorship is meant to look like for the patient.</p>

<p>Cancer survivorship reflects the patient’s experience with cancer and cancer treatment, and the physical, emotional and social effects that has on their life. Survivorship care is designed to identify and address the <a href="https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cncr.70039">complex needs of a cancer survivor</a> beyond just the physical changes. It involves coordinating care and promoting the person’s overall health and well-being.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Patient lying on exam table as ultrasound technician places instrument on their neck" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Cancer care requires significant coordination across medical specialties.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/female-doctor-examining-a-patients-neck-by-using-an-royalty-free-image/1473904717">ljubaphoto/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This care can look different for each patient, depending on the cancer they have and their individual needs. For example, my team and I designed a survivorship clinic at UPMC in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to address the most common issues head and neck cancer survivors experience. In addition to surgeons and nurses, our team includes swallowing therapists, a physical therapist, a dental care team and a dietitian to help address issues with swallowing, nutrition, dental health, physical function and mood. All of these services are offered at the same location and can be completed in one visit on the same day, generally under one copay.  </p>

<p>After the visit, the cancer survivor, their oncology team and their primary care clinician receive a care plan to help coordinate care and communication among all their providers. Rather than as a one-time session, our survivorship clinic builds relationships with survivors, supporting them as their needs change over time.</p>

<h2>Timing matters for cancer survivorship</h2>

<p>While a person becomes a survivor at the time of diagnosis, most survivorship care is delivered after the initial treatment has ended. This may be partly because to be accredited by a major medical body that sets cancer care standards, the American College of Surgeons <a href="https://www.facs.org/quality-programs/cancer-programs/commission-on-cancer/standards-and-resources/">Commission on Cancer</a>, hospitals must offer at least three services to cancer survivors after they complete their initial treatment.</p>

<p>While survivorship care can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11764-021-01128-1">ease physical and psychological issues</a> after cancer treatment, survivors often report <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00034894231154182">significant unmet needs</a> before and during treatment.</p>

<p>In my specialty of head and neck cancers, many patients undergo a grueling five to seven weeks of radiation therapy, often in addition to chemotherapy. They experience a host of side effects: pain, mouth sores, skin burns, difficulty swallowing and weight loss, which together can lead to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaoto.2025.4203">treatment interruption and hospitalization</a>. These side effects often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.34861">continue and sometimes worsen years after treatment</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Close-up of person holding hand to their neck" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Treatment for head and neck cancer can come with significant side effects.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-with-thyroid-gland-problem-royalty-free-image/1855047943">Pony Wang/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>While our survivorship clinic was initially designed for patients who completed treatment, we later expanded our services to patients before radiation. We previously found that starting survivorship care before radiation was associated with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00520-025-09797-9">better quality of life and reduced symptoms</a>.</p>

<p>In our newly published research, we found that among 471 cancer survivors, 62% of those who attended our survivorship clinic before <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3198">completing radiation finished treatment on time</a>, compared with 48% of those who were not seen before completing radiation. At three years, 60% of patients seen in the survivorship clinic before completing radiation were alive and cancer-free, compared with 39% of those not seen before completion. The association remained after accounting for whether patients completed radiation on time, suggesting that on-time completion may not fully explain the difference.</p>

<p>Although our results suggest that shifting the start of survivorship care to before treatment may improve outcomes, they do not prove it. Our team plans to test in a larger clinical trial whether starting survivorship care before radiation helps patients finish treatment on time and maintain quality of life, while also examining how teams coordinate care and referrals.</p>

<h2>Survivorship care is not universal</h2>

<p>Comprehensive cancer care implies not only a comprehensive treatment plan, but also supportive care that will help patients live well beyond their diagnosis and treatment. However, a 2024 survey of 384 facilities accredited by the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer found that only 1 in 5 programs estimated that most of their eligible patients <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.18736">receive survivorship care</a>.</p>

<p>For head and neck cancer survivors specifically, nearly all clinicians routinely assess cancer recurrence, swallowing and thyroid function. But only about half <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/hed.26066">address psychological symptoms</a>, such as anxiety and depression, and fewer than 1 in 3 addressed body image or sleep problems.</p>

<p>Survivorship care is often framed as care that begins after treatment ends, which can delay patients’ access to support during treatment. Communication breakdowns may leave patients unaware of available services, while a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.18736">lack of referrals</a> can keep them from receiving needed care. Survivorship care also draws on clinicians with different areas of expertise, and some hospitals and treatment centers may lack enough dedicated staff time to provide a full range of services.</p>

<h2>Thinking ahead in cancer care</h2>

<p>The end of treatment is a huge milestone that patients and their loved ones reach for. But it is not where survivorship care truly starts. </p>

<p>Making survivorship care more accessible may help make cancer care more comprehensive. Clinicians and researchers can start planning for the survivor’s life after cancer even when it’s not on the patient’s mind. Bringing a team that combines treatment experts with rehabilitation and supportive care specialists into the room early can help achieve better outcomes for patients. </p>

<p>As a cancer survivor or a loved one, you don’t need to wait.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294431/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

She directs the UPMC Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Clinic, which was the setting for the research described in this article.</span></em></p></content>

title: Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India
