<title>Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767254/original/file-20261020-60-3j88qu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1023%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, right, and Neha Bora, president of the All India Students&#39; Association, address a press conference in New Delhi on Oct. 15, 2026.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/India%20Protests/3cd36859ca62481e8720af80d2fc8bf6/photo">AP Photo/Manish Swarup</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Five months <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/asia/india-cockroach-janta-party.html">after its founding</a>, India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain. </p>

<p>The movement was formed in May 2026 to protest the government’s cancellation of medical school entrance exams and after India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant likened unemployed youth to cockroaches. By July, the largely Gen Z movement had <a href="https://indianexpress.com/article/india/cjp-protest-dharmendra-pradhan-resigns-education-minister-10803141/">scored an early victory</a> with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.   </p>

<p>The CJP has since moved on to a much larger political issue: critics’ claims that the Election Commission has <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/14/india-protests-election-commission-gyanesh-kumar">deleted approximately 130 million names</a> from the voter rolls. Since Oct. 2, protesters have descended on the streets of Delhi, Mumbai and other cities demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, halting the deletions pending an independent inquiry, and the restoration of the old electoral rolls before the next elections. </p>

<p>In the process, the CJP has encountered <a href="https://www.reuters.com/graphics/INDIA-POLITICS/POLICING/znvngnxmdpl/">strong government resistance.</a>. Amid a crackdown on protests, two of the movement’s spokespersons – Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das – <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/india/indian-court-extends-custody-cockroach-movement-leaders-local-media-says-2026-10-19/">were detained</a>, while Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his right-wing populist Bharatiya Janata Party have refused to bend on the voter roll issue – instead accusing protesters of undermining democracy. </p>

<p>Nonetheless, as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ZsoF5nQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">long-time scholar of Indian political parties and social movements</a>, I believe the CJP’s protests have revealed people’s deep-seated anxieties over democratic erosion in a country of nearly 1.5 billion. Through courage and acerbic wit, the CJP has done something that has eluded conventional opposition parties over the past 12 years: puncturing the ruling party’s <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/08/01/cockroaches-protests-gen-z-india-delhi-narendra-modi-prime-minister/">aura of invulnerability</a>. In doing so, I believe the protests have challenged the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized. </p>

<h2>Defining ‘democracy’ and ‘the people’</h2>

<p>Modi <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2026-10-13/modi-says-india-is-the-mother-of-democracy-video">often describes</a> India as the “Mother of Democracy,” a reference to its civilizational heritage and to Bharat Mata, the Hindu mother goddess. Democracy, he insists, is not a Western import but a native inheritance. The implication is meant to be reassuring: Modern India has always been democratic and always will be.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A crowd of protesters holding India's national flag walks in a procession on the streets." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767255/original/file-20261020-50-2m171k.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Workers and activists of various opposition parties march toward the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi on Oct. 12, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/India%20Protests/fd8c65bc714d4ca8b722568cf5c0bdb2/photo">AP Photo/Manish Swarup</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But some outside monitors disagree. Sweden’s V-Dem Institute classifies India as an “<a href="https://www.indiancentury.org/research-papers/inside-the-v-dem-rankings">electoral autocracy</a>,” meaning that although it regularly holds multiparty elections, it fails basic democratic benchmarks such as legislative and judicial checks and balances and citizens’ active political participation. </p>

<p>Judged by how the country treats dissent, the record is damning: using anti-terrorism laws <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/india-security-terrorism-laws-used-to-silence-dissent/a-75534044">to jail activists without trial</a>, barricading protest sites, <a href="https://www.techpolicy.press/indias-decentralized-system-of-internet-censorship/">internet blackouts</a> and <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/india/un-experts-urge-indian-authorities-cease-use-excessive-force-curb-protests-2026-10-20/">police brutality</a>. </p>

<p>By contrast, the CJP considers peaceful protest, along with upholding the country’s constitution, essential elements of democracy. Demonstrators regularly circulate images of <a href="https://www.constitutionofindia.net/members/b-r-ambedkar/">B. R. Ambedkar</a> – the chief architect of the Indian constitution – on posters, in slogans and in songs. Like Ambedkar, 30-year-old CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke is a Dalit, or untouchable within the Hindu caste system.</p>

<p>Critics argue that the Bharatiya Janata Party defines the nation through <a href="https://www.bjp.org/chapter-2">Hindu civilizational identity</a>, which is exclusionary because it rejects India’s rich Muslim historical traditions and casts doubt on the political loyalties of the country’s Muslims, who constitute about <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2021/09/21/population-growth-and-religious-composition/">14% of the population</a> – 197 million people. By contrast, the CJP draws no line between insider and outsider by faith, caste or birth, and it defines community by shared commitments. </p>

<p>The voter roll struggle shows what is at stake in the question. The Election Commission says the revision will remove duplicate entries, deceased voters <a href="https://indianexpress.com/article/express-exclusive/election-commission-sir-14-objections-gyanesh-kumar-sukhbir-singh-sandhu-vivek-joshi-10889737/">and noncitizens</a>. But critics worry that the burden of proof falls on voters. Consider how hard it is for poor Muslims, Dalits and migrant workers to produce decades-old birth, education and land certificates. Moreover, those whose names are struck from the electoral rolls fear being branded <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/14/india-protests-election-commission-gyanesh-kumar">illegal immigrants</a>. </p>

<h2>Cracks appear in Bharatiya Janata Party’s dominance</h2>

<p>While the Bharatiya Janata Party had held the prime minister’s office before, Modi’s 2014 election marked a sea change in Indian politics, disrupting the Congress Party’s dominance. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The BJP owed it electoral success in part to attracting young and first-time voters with promises of employment, economic growth and what is known in Hindi as “<a href="https://www.reuters.com/article/world/us-politics/where-are-the-good-days-challenges-mount-for-indias-modi-idUSKCN1M10XG/">achhe din aane waale hain</a>,” or “good days are coming.” Since the BJP took office in 2014, the country has charted strong GDP growth, but the macroeconomic success <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-68823827">has been belied</a> by ongoing and rampant inequality that falls especially hard on the poor and young.</p>

<p>The BJP claims to have fulfilled some of its more targeted campaign promises, such as engaging in merit-based <a href="https://www.financialexpress.com/india-news/under-bjp-government-jobs-being-given-purely-on-merit-basis-says-haryana-cm-manohar-lal-khattar/1100415/">public sector hiring</a>. Yet 40% of Indian college graduates <a href="https://thewire.in/labour/nearly-40-of-indian-graduates-under-the-age-of-25-are-unemployed-azim-premji-report">under 25 are unemployed</a>. Paradoxically, the unemployment rate for youth who cannot read and write hovers around just 3.4%. For college graduates, who are the Cockroach Janta Party’s main constituency, it is nearly nine times higher <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-03-29/young-indians-more-likely-to-be-jobless-if-they-re-educated">at roughly 29%</a>.</p>

<p>Seizing on this building discontent, the CJP uses the slogan “Achhe Din” ironically, on posters and memes. Its manifesto opens: “If you are going to call us cockroaches, the least you can do is pay our rent.” It calls for making “lazy” – a code word for the unemployed – a protected political identity. </p>

<p>Underlying the joke is a serious point: that stigmatization of the jobless offends millions of impoverished people, something critics note is protected in the dignity and equality guarantees of articles <a href="https://indiankanoon.org/doc/1199182/">21</a> and<a href="https://indiankanoon.org/doc/367586/">14</a> of the Constitution. </p>

<h2>Who speaks for women?</h2>

<p>The Bharatiya Janata Party has gained women’s electoral support through a combination of targeted welfare schemes, support for increased women’s representation in legislatures and endless talk of women’s empowerment, or <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/5AC0841ABB6D7B5FFB85F680BB608F8B/S2977017326102126a.pdf/nari_shakti_womens_power_and_hindu_nationalism.pdf">“nari shakti</a>.” </p>

<p>However, masses of women protesters have challenged state-defined women’s empowerment. They stop police vans carrying detainees, scale barricades and criticize the prime minister. </p>

<p>One of the most prominent among them is Neha Bora, a Ph.D. student and president of the left-wing All India Students’ Association, whose blunt messages to Modi has seen her profile skyrocket. Modi has said he has been subject to vulgar abuses by the protesters and was shocked by how “our daughters” could use such foul language, but he viewed them as “misdirected children” and was ready <a href="https://www.telegraphindia.com/india/culture-shock-over-daughters-using-foul-language-but-ready-to-forgive-pm-modi-prnt/cid/2172744">to forgive them</a>. </p>

<p>The throngs of women who are protesting express deep discontent with the government’s paternalism. They challenge its Hindu-inflected understanding of empowerment and insist on speaking for themselves rather than being spoken for. They express outrage at the government’s brutal response to their peaceful protests. They describe how the police have beaten and sexually harassed them, while anonymous self-styled guardians of religious morality engage in doxing, threats of rape and acid attacks, and circulate demeaning AI-generated images of them. For protesters, that record sits uneasily besides the prime minister’s denunciation of<a href="https://www.dw.com/en/india-independence-day-modi-condemns-violence-against-women/a-69945477"> violence against women</a>. </p>

<h2>‘Cockroaches never die’</h2>

<p>The CJP motto, “Cockroaches never die,” has wide resonance. Protesters have survived, but not escaped, violence, incarceration, internet blackouts and police blockades. The sunglass-wearing cockroach mascot makes a mockery of leader-centered nationalist branding.</p>

<p>Recent <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-gen-z-led-uprisings-across-asia-reveal-about-the-strengths-and-limitations-of-youth-protest-265706">youth-led uprisings in Bangladesh and Nepal</a> have shown how quickly online mobilization can outrun official control. What distinguishes the CJP is that it pairs humor with legal and technical infrastructure. Its online portal <a href="https://www.cockroachjantaparty.org/saakshi">Saakshi vault</a>, which means “witness,” collects photos and videos of police violence that protesters upload; volunteer lawyers use these to issue complaints against officers.</p>

<p>The CJP’s recent and remarkable successes do not mean that the movement is likely to disrupt the BJP’s hold on power in the next parliamentary elections in 2029. For now at least, the CJP is fairly concentrated in urban strongholds and would need to build organizational infrastructure and develop long-term demands.</p>

<p>However, a generation that a government minister wrote off as lazy and expendable has exposed the cracks in the system that the chief justice defended. Whatever form it takes, the movement provides a vision and reminder of what democracy looks like.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294730/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Would a Democratic Congress change course on Israel?
excerpt: Pro-Palestinian Jewish American demonstrators rally outside AIPAC’s the Manhattan headquarters in February 2024. | Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images This sto
body: Pro-Palestinian Jewish American demonstrators rally outside AIPAC’s the Manhattan headquarters in February 2024. | Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Israel felt inescapable in the midterm primaries, especially for Democrats, where centrists and progressives clashed — memorably! — over military aid, Gaza, and (of course) AIPAC
But with the Election Day almost upon us, the subject seems less prominent
When I Googled “Israel US elections” this morning, all the top results concerned next week’s Israeli parliamentary elections
In less than two weeks, however, Americans will also head to the polls
They’ll decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices

The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits.  As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms
We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November
Previously, we dug into  how both parties are changing , the bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers , and the politics of high costs
This week, we’re tackling Americans’ growing disillusionment with Israel — and how that will (or won’t) show up at the midterm ballot box

Go a little deeper View Link You know the first part of this story already, because we’ve discussed it quite a lot : Americans’ views of Israel have nosedived over the past 18 months.  That shift helped  shape the Democratic primaries and will likely figure prominently in the coming presidential contest
But how much Israel matters in a general midterm election, to people outside the political left…well, November will really test that
Voters rarely rank Israel policy among their top priorities

In a poll that the Associated Press and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research  conducted earlier this month, about 80 percent of registered voters said Congress should highly prioritize the cost of living during its next term, and roughly 70 percent said the same about ending the Iran war
By comparison, less than a third of voters said they prioritized cutting off aid to Israel.  There’s another way that Israel factors into US elections, of course — and that’s in fundraising

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has become one of the biggest spenders in US elections and  a repeat flash point in this year’s Democratic primaries.  But in the general election, even AIPAC has been overshadowed by the GOP’s big-business donors , many of them in tech, who have given Republicans a historic spending advantage in this year’s contests
On Wednesday, the lobbying group actually announced it would no longer endorse political candidates or make direct campaign contributions
In either case, whatever happens in the midterms won’t likely transform US policy toward Israel

President Donald Trump is still in charge of foreign policy, after all, and even if Democrats take back the House, they’ll have little ability to reverse his agenda.  But a Democratic majority would gain “new congressional tools to act on Israel-Palestine issues,” Hady Amr, the former US Special Representative for Palestinian Affairs, wrote in a new analysis for Chatham House
Those tools aren’t flashy (think: hearings, funding restrictions, and reporting requirements), but they could certainly set the stage for a broader policy shift under a Democratic president

Races to watch: Florida’s Senate race , where Democrat Angie Nixon has criticized her party’s ties to the pro-Israel lobby; Michigan’s Senate race, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign  grew out of pro-Palestinian activism ;  Michigan’s (deeply purple) Seventh District , where progressive William Lawrence has vocally criticized US support for Israel.  More from Vox:  The left is winning the argument on aid to Israel
The first true swing-state test for the Bernie left What American Jews want from the midterms One link for later ➨ Gather ye roast spuds while ye may
Vegan restaurants appear to be experiencing a downturn of sorts: According to one online directory, the number of establishments fell from 1,717 last October to 1,509 now
But the news isn’t entirely or unambiguously bad

One added pressure on plant-based restauranters, for instance, is growing competition from mainstream restaurants that have started offering vegan dishes.  Before you go… Did you know… that North America’s largest wind farm has more than 900 turbines, each as tall as the Statue of Liberty, and encompasses an area roughly the size of Chicago? title: Can Trump deport Ilhan Omar?
excerpt: Ilhan Omar (D-MN) speaks at a press conference at the US Capitol on January 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Heather Diehl/Getty Images President Donald Trump has
body: Ilhan Omar (D-MN) speaks at a press conference at the US Capitol on January 13, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Heather Diehl/Getty Images President Donald Trump has been attacking Rep
Ilhan Omar (D-MN) since she first entered Congress in 2019

At various points, he’s called for Omar — a progressive lawmaker who came to the United States as a child refugee from Somalia and who is one of Trump’s most vociferous critics — to be investigated, arrested, and deported.  Now, Trump’s Justice Department is seemingly trying to make good on his threats
Last week, Omar’s Washington, DC, home was raided by federal agents from Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement
According to the Wall Street Journal , the raid was part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork with the explicit goal of denaturalizing and deporting her

The timing alone would make the raid unusual — it’s rare for the Justice Department to take action in political cases so close to an election — and as Washington Post immigration reporter Ted Hesson explains, it also feels uncomfortably pretextual. “It’s almost as if the outcome of the investigation has been stated before anything has taken off,” he told Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram.  Hesson joined Sean to talk about the long history of Trump’s attacks on Omar, what the agents might have been looking for, and whether the administration could actually undermine Omar’s citizenship or even deport her
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
What do we know about what federal agents were looking for in Rep

Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, residence? What we’ve learned through our reporting is that the investigation has looked at both her birth date and whether [Omar or her father] may have lied about it on the naturalization application

A second piece is whether, looking at her father’s military service, she was born in Somalia and was there during the civil war and fled with her family as a young child to a refugee camp in Kenya and was there for years before they eventually came to the US as refugees
This is the president of the United States and his administration entering a sitting representative’s home to figure out what her original birthday is
What is the motivation here, to the best of our knowledge? For years, President Trump has criticized Rep

Omar and made unsubstantiated accusations related to immigration fraud.  There have been theories circulating on the far right — again, unsubstantiated — that she had married her brother as part of an immigration fraud scheme
President Trump himself has repeated that
And several top Trump administration officials in the last few months have said that they believe that there is fraud in her background
They’re making these statements prior to there being an investigation, prior to there being evidence put forward

And it’s almost as if the outcome of the investigation has been stated before anything has taken off.  One thing I should say is that while it does appear that they’re looking at her birthdate, when refugees come into the US, it’s extremely common that their birth records are unreliable because people are fleeing countries that are often in disarray, whether it’s due to civil war or other reasons.  Often, nations like Somalia don’t maintain accurate birth records
So it’s common that refugees who’ve left their country as children, spent time in refugee camps, and then come to the US don’t have a solid understanding of when exactly they were born
I don’t know for sure that that’s the case here, but I know that generally when you’re dealing with refugees, that is true
I know there’s a lot we don’t know here, but investigators enter Rep
Potentially they’re looking for some documents that may list her birthday
If they find some information that’s maybe contrary to official government records, what could that mean, in theory? It’s unclear what sort of charges could be brought from this

And part of the question is, was she 17 and a child at the time of that application or was she 18?  Even if it was determined that she was not a child, I don’t believe they would be able to, say, launch a denaturalization process based on that fact alone

And even if they did attempt to do something like that, these things are not taken lightly and it’s a long involved legal process and very uncommon to pursue something like this over something as simple as this sort of paperwork discrepancy
The president has a long history of hating on Somalia and Somali immigrants to this country.  How does this investigation into Rep

Ilhan Omar fit into the president and his administration’s broader efforts to take away American citizenship? In the past year especially, we’ve seen President Trump use really inflammatory and derogatory language to refer to Somali Americans and Somali immigrants in the US
Even for someone who frequently employs anti-immigrant rhetoric, and the president has in his past, some of the things he said went beyond even that
He does seem to have particularly targeted Somalis in the US and Somali Americans, and Rep

Omar has been part of that.  I think what’s interesting here or what could be interesting is that this case wades into different territory of taking somebody who’s a naturalized citizen, who’s been in the US for decades as a citizen, and saying, “We’re potentially going to reopen that and go back and look at your file and see, do we find anything that might be out of line?” The idea that you could do that with someone who’s a sitting lawmaker could mean that you could potentially do that to any other person who may have applied
Now, one thing we’ve learned is that in the case of Rep
Omar, the administration has looked at the idea, in the event that criminal charges can’t be brought, of potentially canceling her citizenship certificate
It’s almost like a fast-track way to disrupt someone’s citizenship.  It doesn’t remove it

You remain a citizen, but you lose the document that is the underlying proof of that, which could then cause problems with federal government documents, and it could even lead to immigration proceedings where the government tries to make the case that you should be deported
Omar responded? Her camp has vociferously pushed back against the allegations

In regard to the search, they’ve actually said that there was a court-ordered guideline that should have been followed, and that involved consulting the counsel for the House of Representatives before the search happened
They said that never happened, and if it had, it would’ve given Rep

Omar perhaps time to prepare for this or some sort of legal recourse.  They’re saying that not only is this continuation of President Trump’s attack on her politically motivated, but also that the actual legal guidelines that were outlined in that search warrant were not followed
Are other Democrats speaking up on her behalf? Former President Barack Obama in particular is one extremely prominent person who came out and made a social media post elevating her case
The interesting part is that President Obama does not often weigh in on public debates like this or is at least measured in the opportunities when he does

title: The 2026 election could reshape healthcare
excerpt: New Yorkers march in support of universal healthcare this summer. | LightRocket via Getty Images Americans are furious about the state of our healthcare system.
body: New Yorkers march in support of universal healthcare this summer. | LightRocket via Getty Images Americans are furious about the state of our healthcare system.  A recent KFF poll found 60 percent of US adults worry about the cost of medical care — more than gasoline, food and groceries, or their rent or mortgage
One in three Americans say they worry every day or almost every day about their ability to afford healthcare, per a new survey from the Pew Research Center

There seems to be a growing appetite for reform, too: More than 65 percent of Americans say they support the government spending more tax dollars to lower healthcare costs.  Democrats are trying to weaponize those frustrations against the Republicans who currently hold Congress and the White House
By a 2-to-1 margin, voters say they trust Democrats over Republicans on healthcare
That could mean single-payer Medicare-for-all or a new public insurance option or maybe something else
What all this energy leads to will depend on what happens in November

The candidates themselves are framing the stakes in those existential terms.  Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems

How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy

Sign up here . “Medicare for all is where we need to go,” Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Michigan Senate race whose support for the policy has been widely covered, said during an August interview with CNN. “And my hope is, both coming out of the 2026 midterms and then out of 2028, that we’re going to be on our way to a Senate majority to be able to get this done.” Real change will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election and a new occupant in the White House

But this year’s midterms are still a make-or-break moment: The candidates who get elected this year, and how they shape the upcoming presidential primary debate and actions in Congress, will determine whether healthcare reform happens at all.  If you’re fed up with the state of American healthcare, and you want to see a change, you should show up for the midterms on Tuesday, November 3

Big midterm wins can beget big healthcare wins  The classic pattern in American elections is that more voters go to the polls during presidential campaigns than during the midterm elections when only House and Senate seats are on the ballot
Turnout has started to tick up for the midterms in recent years, but it still trails behind presidential years
Midterms suffer from the perception that there’s not as much at stake if the White House is not on the line
But that’s never been strictly true.  Midterm elections are extraordinarily important in shaping the future of policymaking, even if the payoff is delayed

They help determine both the character of the Congress that could eventually pass a major bill after the next presidential election, and the kind of ideas and policies that are going to be prioritized. “Voters should see 2026 and 2028 as the elections that will guide the next big change in our healthcare system,” said Natalie Davis , CEO and co-founder of the advocacy group United States of Care, in a statement to Vox. “These elections will be how voters’ demands are heard — and will tell us whether the next real window for change will come with serious reforms or missed opportunity.” A walk through the recent history of healthcare reform should help make the stakes of the 2026 elections clear
In 2006, the national mood looked similar to what we’re seeing today
A very unpopular Republican president was in office, and the country had soured on his agenda
Bush’s foreign wars and his misguided attempt to overhaul Social Security gave Democrats an opportunity to win big in the 2006 midterms — and they did
Dems won more than 30 seats and secured a comfortable majority in the House
In the Senate , they won six seats and narrowly took control of that chamber too
It was a resounding rejection of the Bush administration, and it set up the next decade of Democratic policymaking

At the highest level, the midterms gave energy to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, united as they were around their opposition to the Iraq War, and that energy carried over to the presidential primary
Barack Obama defeated Hillary Clinton and won the presidency, springboarding off of the excitement that started with the 2006 elections
Dems’ success in the midterms also helped put lowering healthcare costs at the forefront of the Democratic agenda

That encouraged both Obama and Clinton to develop detailed healthcare policy proposals during their primary campaigns and ultimately set the stage for the Democrats to pursue the Affordable Care Act once they had full control of the government in 2009
And then there is the literal size of the congressional majorities that parties need to pass their agenda

Voters may not spend much time thinking about whip counts, but one or two elections in a midterm year can ultimately decide the fate of the next president’s agenda.  Part of the reason Democrats were able to pass the ACA was that they built on their huge wins in 2006 with more wins in 2008 and held massive congressional majorities once Obama was sworn in
And once the debate over healthcare reform really got started, they needed every single vote
It was especially important in the Senate: Democrats had exactly 60 votes in 2009
That meant if all of them united together, they could pass filibuster-proof legislation — so long as nobody defected

That was only possible because in 2006 Mark Pryor won a Senate seat in Arkansas, Sherrod Brown triumphed in a Senate race in Ohio, and Jon Tester beat an incumbent Republican in Montana.  Without those wins in 2006, the Democratic legislative agenda in 2009 would probably have looked different
They might’ve had to pursue a more limited healthcare reform plan; maybe the ACA wouldn’t have passed at all
What kind of Democrats will be on the rise in 2028? The 2006 midterms both created the opportunity for the ACA — and set the limits on what the legislation could actually achieve
Democrats had that 60-seat Senate majority, but within it were many more moderate members
Policies like the public option (which would have authorized the government to create its own health insurance plan to sell alongside private insurance) couldn’t get sufficient support

That is the dilemma of policymaking: You need those swing-seat members to win, which often means tacking to the center, but you also can’t pass anything they won’t get on board with.  Nevertheless, that is a good kind of political problem to have, one which Democrats would be thrilled to face in January 2029
What are we going to do now? It all starts with the vote count
Most projections expect the Democrats to win between 10 and 20 House seats
But the difference between 10 and 20 could be substantial
The cushier the majority, the further you can push the policy agenda

title: How the biggest renewable energy project in US history finally got built
excerpt: When the sun goes down, the wind picks up in central New Mexico, whipping through arid canyons with a ghostly howl that for centuries, locals have likened to th
body: When the sun goes down, the wind picks up in central New Mexico, whipping through arid canyons with a ghostly howl that for centuries, locals have likened to the wails of the folkloric ghost La Llorona.  A few hours east of Albuquerque, this June, those gusts began powering the largest wind farm this continent has ever seen, twirling over 900 colossal steel turbines
Each is as tall as the Statue of Liberty, scattered across a patch of desert roughly the size of Chicago

They plug into a 550-mile transmission line stitched across the Southwest and are now powering over one million homes — as far away as California.  The SunZia Wind and Transmission project is a rare 21st-century triumph of American infrastructure, an engineering marvel that generates more electricity than the Hoover Dam

When the turbines came online this spring, they immediately broke records for wind-generated power in California’s energy supply, where solar power may rule the day, but the winds of New Mexico increasingly fuel the night
Key takeaways SunZia, the largest clean energy megaproject in US history, finally came online this June, sending New Mexico wind power to customers in Arizona and California
For over a decade and a half, the project was delayed by permitting issues, lawsuits, and above all, an energy market that wasn’t ready for the power it had to offer
With the nation’s electricity demand skyrocketing, SunZia’s collaboration with conservationists may offer a blueprint for getting more megaprojects built
After years of stagnant power growth, the US is absolutely starving for more electricity, with demand projected to rise by 25 percent by the end of this decade , and a staggering 78 percent by 2050

Enormous as this challenge might seem, it may ultimately be the catalyst the country needs to dramatically dial up its renewable energy infrastructure, so that the years to come are powered not by gas or coal, but by clean energy sources like the sun and the wind
By next summer, the project will have prevented about 9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from entering the atmosphere, according to Pattern Energy, the project’s developer

For decades, however, it seemed the project would remain little more than a spectral dream.  “It works!” This was the call Hunter Armistead, Pattern’s CEO, remembers getting from his head engineer when the turbines came online for the very first time. “We were creating power, and it was showing up 550 miles away in Phoenix, almost as if it was magic.” During the ribbon-cutting for the wind farm, some construction workers showed off massive new turbine tattoos. “It’s their pride that for the rest of their lives, they can drive by and tell their kid, ‘I did this,’” Armistead said
But SunZia almost didn’t get built at all
It is not just the project’s scale that makes it remarkable, but the utter morass its developers slogged through to bring it online

The project spanned five presidential administrations, an ownership change, a major reroute, and a standoff with a US military base.  It also involved a series of lawsuits from local tribal communities and environmental advocates, some of which remain pending even as the turbines now finally whirl
Building any renewable megaproject requires vast amounts of space, and hyperspecific natural conditions, like a wind that blows at night or a reliably sun-soaked desert plain

Then getting that energy to major cities means traversing some of the most pristine, spectacular natural corridors this nation has left, and particularly in the Southwest, rubbing up against the sacred lands of local tribal communities.  The decades-long saga to settle some of these tensions has turned SunZia into a helpful lesson, and for many, deserved or not, it became the ultimate poster child for permitting reform
And for many years, the country’s need for power didn’t seem to call for such a wildly ambitious project anyway
But in the interim, as the world changed, SunZia changed too, becoming — at least in some places — a better and more collaborative project than it was when it began
And now, with a nation finally focused on building more clean energy megaprojects, it can offer a glimpse of what’s to come, even a blueprint of what could be

The real reason(s) it took so long for SunZia to get built When SunZia was first proposed in 2006, the same year Twitter went online, coal was still the most important electricity source in America, and the nation’s appetite for electricity had remained nearly flat year after year
And for the next 17 years, SunZia flailed, never even breaking ground
It ping-ponged between financial and regulatory purgatories that most commentators have attributed to endless permitting delays
There were, for example, a few state-level permitting debacles , with New Mexico rejecting SunZia’s initial transmission route in 2018
Even after such interstate power lines get federal approval, they often need to wait years longer for approvals from every state in which their project passes
Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, for one, has cited SunZia as a key impetus for his co-sponsoring the Senate’s new plan for permitting reform

This would make it easier for the federal government to coordinate approval processes for interstate transmission lines, ensuring that they happen concurrently and preventing one state from dragging its heels.  The project had faced one particularly large and sticky permitting challenge: getting the power through the White Sands Missile Range
But this, and other challenges, were eventually resolved relatively quickly

And to David Hayes, who served as deputy secretary of the Department of the Interior during the Obama administration, this suggests that financing hamstrung the project even more than red tape.  “The facts are the facts, and they got their permit ,” said Hayes — all the way back in 2015, not long after the Obama administration put SunZia on a “fast-track” to approval. “So we finally got the permit done
Nothing happens.” Part of that was the fact that the two states where SunZia wanted to build its transmission lines were not entirely on board
But it was also the sheer expense involved in building the project, especially given that the federal approval required burying parts of the transmission line near the missile range

Moreover, even if everything went perfectly with the project’s permitting process, it might have been impossible to build SunZia back then, said Armistead, because “we really didn’t have the market need for it.”  The US simply wasn’t as ravenous for new electricity as it is right now, and the importance of building out the future of energy was not enticing enough for investors on its own
But, refusing to die a slow death of a thousand permitting blockades or financial setbacks, SunZia instead evolved
Pattern Energy, initially only in charge of developing the wind farm portion of the project, took over the transmission line project in 2022

Around that time, SunZia applied for a revised federal permit, one that would circumvent the missile range, and within less than two years — a relative sprint for federal bureaucracy — they had a new approval in hand
Then came $11 billion in financing from several global financial institutions, pension funds, and clean energy investors
Then, a few years of construction time later, the Americas’ biggest wind farm was finally switched on

And more massive projects like this will be needed because nowadays, “there is no longer the excuse” of a market unready for high volumes of clean energy, Armistead told me. “It is game time, and we’re supposed to get this done.” What America’s biggest clean energy project got right One of the secrets to SunZia’s ultimate success in New Mexico was the project’s ability to strike compromises, even with some of its earliest critics

In some cases, a bunch of birds.  Right about now, the earliest migratory birds, like the crimson-capped sandhill crane, have begun arriving at their Southwestern wintering grounds, not far from some of SunZia’s newly operational high-voltage transmission lines
This crane had nearly gone extinct before, driven in part by an explosion of new hydroelectric dams in the early 20th century, whose construction dried out local wetlands

SunZia’s initial route, which was planned across one of the most congested flyways in the country, threatened them again, birders feared, alongside other migratory species who might accidentally fly into the new power lines, a threat believed to kill millions of birds nationwide each year.  While SunZia’s original developer, the Southwestern Power Group, was largely unmoved by those concerns, said Sarah Rose, vice president of climate at the National Audubon Society, the nonprofit found an unusually receptive partner to compromise when Pattern Energy took over.  “They took their role as a project developer really seriously,” she said, “and I think they engaged with us with a lot of integrity and a lot of good faith.” Under a rerouting plan, original power lines were moved north, erected next to existing infrastructure, or affixed with visual warning systems or bird diverters

title: You’re supposed to get one free doctor’s visit every year. So why are so many Americans being charged?
excerpt: After moving to West Virginia last year, Steve Kuo signed up for a new insurance plan that would cost him $500 a month
body: After moving to West Virginia last year, Steve Kuo signed up for a new insurance plan that would cost him $500 a month
But there was one upside: He knew he was entitled to a free preventive visit
He wanted to take advantage of it, so he made an appointment at a clinic near his new home
But then when he got there, they asked about his medical history and he mentioned prior kidney problems
When he received a bill a few weeks later, he had been charged twice for the same appointment: Once as that free preventive visit, once as an “office sick visit” because of the kidney conversation

He was flummoxed — and very annoyed, as he shared on social media. “No copayment means no copayment, exactly as stated in the insurance guidelines,” Kuo told me over email. “What is written and agreed upon should be honored.” He is far from alone

On Reddit, I easily found more than a dozen examples in just the past year of people getting a surprise bill for what they thought was going to be a free visit.  One woman posted a nearly $1,000 bill she’d received for what she thought was going to be a preventive gynecology visit

Another woman said that she ended up facing roughly $3,000 bills because she was given an ultrasound (which she said she didn’t request) at a preventive visit, and then her blood draw was sent to an out-of-network lab
Another person lamented that they had been billed $170 for an office visit because they had briefly mentioned back stiffness

Americans don’t get much when it comes to our healthcare, but most of us are supposed to be entitled to at least one thing: Once every year, no matter your health insurance, you can go to the doctor with the goal of preventing future health problems by discussing important vaccinations, cancer screenings, and cardiovascular health screenings
The Affordable Care Act made that the law in 2010

But more than 15 years later, people all over the country are walking into their doctor’s office, thinking they’re entitled to that one free visit every year, and walking out being billed for a sick visit, blood labs, and more
Researchers estimate that Americans spend tens of millions, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars every year on services that are supposed to be free under the ACA

Yalda Jabbarpour , a family physician in the Washington, DC, area and medical director of the Robert Graham Center for Policy Studies, told me she still deals all the time with people’s confusion about what a preventive visit really means. “Every single time I’m in the clinic, this issue comes up with a patient
And it’s sad that it comes up,” Jabbarpour told me. “In my mind, the blame is not to be put on the patient
The blame is not to be put on the physician

Really, this points to a bigger system issue that we need to solve.” How could a seemingly simple promise of one free annual doctor’s visit result in a situation so convoluted that patients and doctors are still struggling with it nearly two decades later? And how might we fix it? Patients are getting surprise bills from their doctors — and they’re pissed off The goal of the ACA was to expand coverage and make sure health insurance would be comprehensive to actually help people stay healthy
As part of that project, the authors of the law added a mandate for insurers to cover those services, including an annual wellness exam

The problem is, they did not define what the parameters of that preventive visit actually were, said Alex Hoagland , a healthcare economist at the University of Toronto.  “It didn’t establish a clear definition of…all the diagnosis codes and procedure codes and how frequently you get that combination within a year,” he said. “They don’t define what actually is preventive care and what’s not.” Do’s and don’t’s for a preventive visit: Topics that should be free to talk about: routine vaccinations, many cancer screenings, screenings for diabetes and cardiovascular health, contraception
Topics that could lead to you getting charged: chronic pain, prior medical problems, other physical and mental health symptoms (including depression)
If you are a first-time visitor at a doctor’s office, you may also be charged a “new patient” fee
That has left each insurer to define a preventive visit on their own — and that’s where the perverse incentives that leave patients in a lurch begin

Preventive visits are supposed to be reserved strictly for screenings and talking about other preventive measures you can take to protect your long-term health, but you may get billed for an “office visit” or a “sick visit” if you talk about any specific symptom you’re experiencing, the same as if you had come in because you had the flu.  Health insurers have an incentive to keep the definition of preventive care as narrow as possible, so they have to pay fewer claims without any contribution from the patient
At the same time, doctors want to be paid for the actual services that they are providing

If somebody does bring up a bigger health problem during a preventive visit, then the doctor reasonably wants to be paid accordingly.  “I know, particularly in the healthcare space, it’s really popular to blame one party or another, and here I don’t think it’s a matter of corporate greed or physician incompetence or whatever,” Hoagland said. “It’s just a natural mismatch of incentives.” So the reality is that “one free doctor’s visit” sounds straightforward, but, in practice, it’s much more complicated
You as the patient might think of it as one visit, but in our fee-for-service healthcare system, where providers bill based on each specific thing they do, it’s not
The conversation about your vaccination may be free — but asking about your back pain is not
If you get blood tests ordered, that’s another line item

The list goes on. “It’s not like you walk into a doctor’s office and it’s just one thing that happens, right?” said Sabrina Corlette , co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University. “It’s multiple different things that are happening when you go into a doctor’s office.” Part of the problem may be that it’s one free visit
We Americans are consumers at heart: Tell us we’re going to get something for free and we want to take advantage of it

But having just one free visit may also lead to people bringing a laundry list of questions to that preventive visit, because they think of it as their only chance to ask everything of their doctor.  That makes it easy for the discussion to tip over into a sick visit — and not only does that lead to a surprise bill, it can also crowd out the conversation about prevention that the visit is supposed to be focused on. “What ends up happening a lot…is that a patient comes in for their annual visit, and in their mind, that is their time to bring up every single thing that’s been happening during the year, because they see it as the free visit to bring up everything that’s happened during the year

For some patients, that takes up the entire visit,” Jabbarpour told me. “They leave, and it’s like, ‘Oh my god, we forgot to do all the screening things: the vaccinations, the cancer screenings, and the cardiovascular risk screening.’ And then something happens down the line because you never address those screenings.” A 2021 study by Hoagland and Paul Shafer, both of Boston University at the time, estimated that Americans with employer-sponsored insurance had in 2018 alone paid between $75 million and $219 million in medical bills that should have been free
They were more likely to be charged for things like contraception or cholesterol and diabetes screenings, with individuals sometimes paying hundreds of dollars for those services
Hoagland told me he had been billed for preventive visits because he has type 1 diabetes and the system automatically categorized his appointment as a diabetic visit
Earlier this year, he co-authored a study that found people with chronic conditions were more likely to be charged for preventive care
Corlette said that she too had recently been charged for what was supposed to be a preventive visit after she mentioned an issue as an aside

And these are folks who study health care for a living. “It was literally maybe a 10-second conversation where I would ask the doctor a question about something,” she said. “And that triggered it.” Colonoscopies are another dramatic example of how this issue plays out in real life; Corlette told me the procedure was one of the first services where this fuzzy line between prevention and treatment under the ACA became obvious
People go under for what is supposed to be a preventive colonoscopy

But then their doctor finds a polyp and decides to remove it — good clinical practice, but as a result, their patient could end up being charged thousands of dollars because the colonoscopy was no longer preventive once that polyp was snipped. “All of a sudden, that would trigger what the patient thought was a preventive service into a cost-sharing obligation,” Corlette said. “Colonoscopies can be thousands of dollars

That was when we were first like, ‘Oh, yeah, this is a more complicated area than I think the lawmakers that drafted this provision originally envisioned.’” How the US could fix our preventive visit headaches The ACA’s preventive visit promise was clearly well-intentioned and it’s worth remembering that, if you look in the aggregate, more Americans are getting more free preventive care than they did before the law was passed

title: The Cornell rape case has surfaced a hidden divide among progressives
excerpt: A rally takes place in New York City on October 8, 2026, in the wake of Cornell University rape accusations. | Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images The harrowin
body: A rally takes place in New York City on October 8, 2026, in the wake of Cornell University rape accusations. | Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images The harrowing allegations of rape at a Cornell University fraternity have been rippling out in both New York state and national politics
Democrats have tended to voice sympathy with the accuser, saying that they stand with her and other victims
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) said there was “a culture of rape, sexual assault, and pedophilia” in elite institutions across the country

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Cornell “protected her abusers, letting them off with a slap on the wrist.”  Key takeaways In the wake of the Cornell rape allegations, advocates for victims of rape and sexual assault are renewing a push for New York to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law
This proposed change would make it easier for prosecutors to argue that people can be too intoxicated to consent to sex, even if they are conscious and haven’t explicitly said no

But this reform effort has met resistance from key parts of the progressive coalition who are skeptical of the criminal justice system; they fear new tough laws will be weaponized against minority groups and contribute to mass incarceration
Kathy Hochul said the accuser was “failed” by local police and county prosecutors who did not bring charges, so Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to take over the investigation
Days before that appointment, James posted on social media that “what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” adding: “To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone
We stand with you.”  Some Republicans, meanwhile, are accusing Democrats of rushing to judgment

Saritha Komatireddy, who is running for attorney general of New York against James, said in a debate that James had “screwed this one up by prejudging it.” The investigation, Komatireddy said, “requires someone who approaches the case with fairness, impartiality and integrity.” And right-wing commentators like Megyn Kelly and Ben Shapiro have questioned the accuser’s story

But beyond the procedural fight over this particular investigation, many Democrats have also called for changing the law to make cases like it that involve drugs or alcohol easier to prosecute in general.  This might seem like a clean issue for the party, in line with prior progressive efforts to crack down on sexual assault via Title IX and expanding statute of limitations laws .  However, it’s not so simple: According to my conversations with experts and advocates involved in these reform conversations, this is where the Democratic unity begins to fray, because of a divide between two key parts of the progressive coalition.  The impulse to create stronger protections for victims has crashed into the left’s longstanding suspicion of the criminal justice system
And as a result, a coherent policy response has been hard to craft — and may end up being impossible to get agreement on
On one side are advocacy groups for women and for victims of rape or sexual assault
They argue that current law — in New York and other states — makes it far too difficult to successfully prosecute perpetrators, and that it should be changed
They’ve advocated for closing what they call the “ voluntary intoxication loophole ,” which they say makes it harder to prosecute abusers of victims who have willingly consumed drugs or alcohol
On the other side are various progressive or left constituencies that are deeply skeptical of the criminal justice system

These constituencies — which include key figures in New York’s Black political establishment, public defenders, supporters of criminal justice reform, and members of the Democratic Socialists of America — are united by a shared antipathy to mass incarceration and what they see as disproportionate police targeting of minority communities.  The former camp argues that false rape and sexual assault allegations are vanishingly rare, that these crimes are hugely underpunished, and that the law needs to be updated to make these prosecutions easier

But the latter camp argues that Black and other nonwhite men are often falsely accused, and that it would be unwise to hand prosecutors another tool they could use to put men in jail in cases where ascertaining consent is more difficult
Modern-day progressives have strongly backed the Me Too movement as well as campaigns for racial justice and criminal justice reform
Progressives want to be on the side of victims against the privileged and powerful — but sometimes, they have different ideas about who falls into which category

The legal issues around “voluntary intoxication” and rape charges, explained The current controversy in New York focuses on efforts to close what advocates call the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in rape and sexual assault law
Every state says it’s a crime to have sex with someone who is unconscious
And every state says it’s a crime to have sex with someone who is incapacitated due to unknowingly being dosed with drugs

But what about someone who chooses to drink or take drugs, who remains conscious, and who doesn’t outright refuse consent? Should there be a standard by which the law deems that person incapable of meaningfully consenting, because they are too intoxicated?  Many states have long had laws on the books saying yes — that someone who voluntarily drinks or does drugs can reach a state where they are too mentally impaired to consent to sex, even if they’re conscious and capable of communicating
But about half of states don’t have such a law, according to the Associated Press
And this hasn’t been an especially partisan issue to this point, with a mix of red and blue states adopting each standard
The push to change the law in New York predates the Cornell case, and goes back to the late 2010s

At that time, the Me Too movement had put Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr. in the hot seat, with advocates criticizing him for not initially prosecuting Harvey Weinstein and arguing he was soft on rape and sex crimes generally.  In the midst of pivoting on the issue (he had Weinstein indicted in 2018), Vance claimed that, in certain of these cases, his office was hamstrung by what he called a “loophole” in New York law involving intoxication. “Prosecutors cannot bring sex crime charges in cases where the victim became voluntarily intoxicated and was unable to consent,” he wrote in a letter
So really, Vance said, it was on the legislature to change the law
Quickly, critics argued that Vance had misstated the law, saying it was not actually true that a loophole allowed people to rape voluntarily intoxicated New Yorkers with impunity

Vance’s office later acknowledged that his initial comments were “inartfully put.”  The problematic cases, Vance’s team argued , were about victims who were “too intoxicated to consent” but who were also at least partially conscious and didn’t outright express their unwillingness — this, they said, was the “gap in the law.” “There’s a real problem that we have with people getting drunk and then being taken advantage of,” Vance said .  So some Democrats and groups advocating for victims of sexual assault and rape kicked off an effort to change that law, in New York and elsewhere

Their favored bill says that lack of consent can be established if an alleged victim is “temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling their conduct” — and if the accused knew or reasonably should have known that

Critics argue, though, that such bills go too far, and could make it easier to prosecute sexual encounters that, to the accused, seemed consensual.  “The proposed legislation fails to provide any objective guidance about when a partner is too intoxicated to legally agree to engage in sexual conduct,” the New York State Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers said in an emailed statement

Skeptics of the bill outlined several scenarios that concerned them, including scenarios where one person seems to consent but later decides that, in retrospect, they were too intoxicated for it to have truly been consensual.  “You get all these scenarios where two people meet up at a bar and they both become voluntarily intoxicated,” said Yung-Mi Lee, a public defender and a former president of New York’s criminal defense lawyers association. “So then, if someone later says, ‘I was voluntarily incapable of appraising my conduct, I lost my inhibitions,’ they could say, ‘You committed a rape against me.’” To advocates for victims’ rights, these concerns are overstated. “The burden that’s placed on a victim of sexual violence is such a large burden to bear in the first place that these changes to the law are really just slightly opening the door,” Rebecca Zipkin of the advocacy group World Without Exploitation told me. “The current situation is not working to provide justice for survivors,” Stefan Turkheimer of RAINN, a network for rape and abuse survivors, told me. “The status quo is not okay.” Why it hasn’t passed in New York Versions of the voluntary intoxication bill have been signed into law in recent years in Minnesota, Michigan, and Texas
The bill has also repeatedly passed the New York state Senate by overwhelming margins
But it has never been brought to a vote in the lower chamber, the New York state Assembly

That’s because, advocates for the bill told me, they’ve faced resistance from some influential parts of the Democratic Party and progressive coalition.  Indeed, the skeptics are said to include two factions that are often at odds: New York’s Black political establishment and the Democratic Socialists of America.  Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie controls which bills come to a vote in his chamber

He was an architect of the state’s sweeping bail reform law , a critic of what he called the existing “racist and classist system,” and has said he would be “a failure as a Black man” if he did not pass criminal justice reform.  “It is generally known that Speaker Heastie does not believe in creating new crimes because he believes New York suffers from overincarceration,” Lizzie Asher, an advocate for changing the law and a co-founder of the Justice Without Exclusion Coalition, told me. (Heastie has said that he did not bring the bill to a vote because it lacked enough support among his chamber’s Democrats.) Assembly member Latrice Walker is another champion of criminal justice reform; she even did a hunger strike in 2023 to protest rollbacks to the bail reform law

She spoke out about her concerns about the voluntary intoxication bill earlier this year, telling the New York Times that while she wanted survivors to get justice, she was “cautious about the creation of new laws and our duty to preserve due process protections.” Zipkin and other advocates have also pointed to the six DSA-affiliated members of the assembly, who are associated with a general skepticism about the criminal justice system and incarceration, as a potential obstacle
None are currently listed as cosponsors of the bill

<title>Chiricahua is the nation’s newest national park – what does that mean?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766817/original/file-20261016-50-ymrfah.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C85%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A large rock balanced atop another is one of the striking features of the Chiricahua landscape.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chiricahua_balanced_rock.jpg">Pretzelpaws via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>With a stroke of a pen, President Donald Trump has officially created the United States’ <a href="https://www.nps.gov/chir/learn/news/chiricahua-national-monument-becomes-america-s-newest-national-park.htm">64th national park</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nps.gov/chir/index.htm">Chiricahua</a>, in southeastern Arizona, was established as a <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/faraway-ranch-chiricahua-national-monument.htm">national monument in April 1924</a> to protect its towering rhyolite hoodoos – tall spires of rock – and diversity of wildlife. The mountainous landscape is commonly known as a “wonderland of rocks.”</p>

<p>An <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6380">act of Congress</a>, signed by Trump, has now designated the 12,000-acre property a national park, the flagship label of the National Park Service system. It joins the <a href="https://www.nps.gov/grca/index.htm">Grand Canyon</a>, <a href="https://www.nps.gov/pefo/index.htm">Petrified Forest</a> and <a href="https://www.nps.gov/sagu/index.htm">Saguaro</a> as the fourth national park in Arizona.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/sethkannarr/">geographer</a> who studies parks and the naming of places, I have seen that when a National Park Service property is redesignated as a national park, the new label doesn’t typically include much change for the site itself beyond signs and branding.</p>

<p>There’s not usually more money available to manage or protect the site. But the new title serves political purposes and could mean quite a lot to visitors, supporters and surrounding communities alike in the coming years.</p>

<h2>How parks are designated</h2>

<p>The National Park Service <a href="https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/national-park-system.htm">manages 433 properties, which it calls units</a>, with <a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/nps-designations.htm">19 different designations</a>, such as “national battlefields,” “national lakeshores” and “national scenic trails.” Only <a href="https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/national-park-system.htm">64 of these units</a> carry the formal title or designation of “national park.”</p>

<p>All but one of these categories can be bestowed only by Congress. National monuments can be created by the president directly, under the provisions of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/national-monuments-have-grown-and-shrunk-under-us-presidents-for-over-a-century-thanks-to-one-law-the-antiquities-act-252707">Antiquities Act of 1906</a>.</p>

<p>For example, the Antiquities Act has been at the center of a decade-long controversy over the size of <a href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/12/28/proclamation-establishment-bears-ears-national-monument">Bears Ears National Monument</a>, which President Barack Obama created to protect 1.3 million acres in Utah in December 2016. That same act allowed Trump to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/apr/08/deb-haaland-bears-ears-national-monument">shrink the protected area to 200,000 acres</a> in 2017 and President Joe Biden to <a href="https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/10/08/a-proclamation-on-bears-ears-national-monument/">reexpand it to 1.3 million acres</a> in 2021. In 2026, <a href="https://www.sltrib.com/news/environment/2026/07/15/here-are-new-maps-bears-ears-grand/">Trump slashed it again, to 121,000 acres</a>.</p>

<iframe src="https://flo.uri.sh/visualisation/30596891/embed" title="Interactive or visual content" class="flourish-embed-iframe" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" style="width:100%;height:600px;" sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-scripts allow-downloads allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation" width="100%" height="400"></iframe>

<div style="width:100%!;margin-top:4px!important;text-align:right!important;"><a class="flourish-credit" href="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30596891/?utm_source=embed&amp;utm_campaign=visualisation/30596891" target="_top"><img alt="Made with Flourish" src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/made_with_flourish.svg"> </a></div>

<h2>Why redesignations make a difference</h2>

<p>My previous analysis of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-74653-6_8">contentious redesignation</a> of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis to <a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/index.htm">Gateway Arch National Park</a> in 2018 found that it was not done to offer additional protection for this monument to the United States’ Western exploration and growth.</p>

<p>Rather, the move was meant to take advantage of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.32469/10355/91514">public significance of the “national park” label</a> and thereby attract more tourists and tourism revenue to the local economy.</p>

<p>The effort to make it a national park was part of a <a href="https://www.archpark.org/updates/news/gateway-arch-national-park-designated-new-name-for-park">local campaign to renovate the underground visitor center</a>, revitalize the park grounds and increase tourism. But the <a href="https://www.congress.gov/115/plaws/publ128/PLAW-115publ128.pdf">law that formalized the change</a> included no additional funding, resources or protections for the Gateway Arch.</p>

<p>Changing the designation contradicted the park service’s own declaration that the term “national park” should be used for an area that “<a href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/nps-designations.htm">contains a variety of resources</a> and encompasses large land or water areas to help provide adequate protection of the resources.” </p>

<p>During congressional hearings, the deputy director of the National Park Service, Robert Vogel, recommended the Gateway Arch not be labeled a national park but rather a national monument, because it “<a href="https://www.doi.gov/ocl/s-1438">is too small and limited</a> in the range of resources the site protects and interprets to be called a national park.”</p>

<p>Gateway Arch National Park is now the smallest-area park in the U.S., at less than 200 acres, and is home to a <a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/planyourvisit/the-significance-of-the-gateway-arch-landscape.htm">large steel arch, an open lawn area, a museum and a single historic building</a> – a courthouse where <a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/planyourvisit/och.htm">one of the Dred Scott trials</a> was heard, along with other civil rights cases.</p>

<p>However, it does not provide opportunities to view wildlife in its natural habitat, spectacular geologic features, diverse outdoor recreation opportunities or a sense of wilderness that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-74653-6_8">the public has come to expect from national parks</a>.</p>

<p>The park’s website admits “<a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/learn/nature/plants.htm">it is unusual for a national park to have no natural plant life</a>” and describes the park as adjacent to the “<a href="https://www.nps.gov/jeff/learn/nature/animals.htm">concrete jungle of downtown St. Louis</a>.”</p>

<p>Although Chiricahua’s <a href="https://www.wbaltv.com/article/chiricahua-national-monument-new-national-park-arizona/74065478">rocky landscapes</a> and archaeological evidence of <a href="https://chiricahuaapachenation.org/">long-standing Indigenous use and occupation</a> more closely resembles what <a href="https://doi.org/10.32469/10355/91514">many people expect for a national park</a>, it likely will receive some of the same <a href="https://www.outsideonline.com/adventure-travel/national-parks/gateway-arch-national-park-46/">public critique</a> that the Gateway Arch and other national parks redesignated during the first Trump administration have received.</p>

<h2>Potential ‘new’ national parks on the horizon</h2>

<p>In rare cases, a community, group or other organization proposes adding an area that is not currently managed by the National Park Service to the system, but that process <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS20158">takes a lot of time</a>.</p>

<p>It is more common to change the formal designation of a property already within the system, as has happened with this redesignation of Chiricahua.</p>

<p>Similarly, Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore became <a href="https://www.nps.gov/indu/index.htm">Indiana Dunes National Park</a> in 2019. That same year, White Sands National Monument in New Mexico became <a href="https://www.nps.gov/whsa/index.htm">White Sands National Park</a>. And in 2020, New River Gorge National River in West Virginia became <a href="https://www.nps.gov/neri/index.htm">New River Gorge National Park and Preserve</a>.</p>

<p>There are redesignation efforts underway seeking to make national parks in other locations as well, including the <a href="https://www.backpacker.com/news-and-events/news/delaware-water-gap-national-park/">Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area</a> in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, <a href="https://tiffany.house.gov/media/press-releases/rep-tiffany-reintroduces-bill-create-wisconsins-first-national-park">Apostle Islands National Lakeshore</a> in Wisconsin, and <a href="https://norton.house.gov/media/press-releases/norton-introduces-bill-rename-rock-creek-park-rock-creek-national-park-0">Rock Creek Park</a> in the District of Columbia.</p>

<p>In my measure, it is simply a waiting game to see whether these National Park Service sites will also be redesignated to national parks.</p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Chiricahua’s landscape has been called a ‘wonderland of rock.’</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/ChiricahuaNationalPark/eed9baa7527f44f7a104acd3d3a828a4/photo">Ron Kerbo/National Park Service via Associated Press</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What will actually change for Chiricahua?</h2>

<p>Making Chiricahua a national park was a bipartisan effort – co-sponsored by Arizona U.S. Reps. Juan Ciscomani, a Republican, and Greg Stanton, a Democrat – that has received some opposition for several reasons.</p>

<p>The complaints have highlighted <a href="https://www.rvtravel.com/if-chiricahua-becomes-a-national-park-expect-crowds-why-that-matters//">fears that the new label will bring increased tourism</a> and overcrowding in what is considered a <a href="https://nationalparkobsessed.com/chiricahua-be-a-national-park/">small park with limited infrastructure</a>. Now that Chiricahua has been redesignated, the potential influx of new visitors in the coming years could affect the more <a href="https://www.rvtravel.com/if-chiricahua-becomes-a-national-park-expect-crowds-why-that-matters/">personal and isolated experience</a> that they currently appreciate.</p>

<p>However, the only real changes in these places would be in marketing – the signs, <a href="https://www.nps.gov/subjects/hfc/a-brief-history-of-the-unigrid.htm">brochures</a> and merchandise sold in gift shops. But these changes have an important effect: The tagline of “new national park” <a href="https://headwaterseconomics.org/public-lands/protected-lands/national-monuments-redesignated-national-parks/">markets well</a> to <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R41816">potential visitors</a>.</p>

<p>But the funding that Chiricahua receives from the federal government will not change, and the label of “national park” won’t actually protect this landscape any better than it already is under the stewardship of the National Park Service.</p>
